title: Empathetic advice-column register
description: This latent fires on the characteristic voice of a supportive, non-judgmental advice-giver (e.g., an AI or advice-column respondent) addressing someone's personal/relationship problem. It captures validating openers ('I'm sorry you had to go through that', 'It's completely reasonable to...'), reassurances of non-judgment ('Please know that I'm not here to judge'), tentative interpretive claims about others' motives or feelings ('It's likely he...', 'This could suggest that...'), encouraging affirmations ('That's a great starting point!', 'I'm so proud of you'), and check-in/engagement questions ('What do you think?', 'How does that sound?') that punctuate this advice-giving discourse. It does NOT track any particular topic (relationships, chores, driving, health advice all appear) but rather the pragmatic stance and rhetorical moves of empathetic, hedged, second-person counseling language. Sentences that merely state neutral facts, instructions, or first-person narrative without this validating/advisory register are excluded, even if topically similar.

title: Empathetic relationship-advice validation and tips
description: This latent fires on the stock language of AI-generated interpersonal/relationship advice responses (e.g., Reddit AITA or relationship-advice answers): validating statements ('It's understandable that...', 'It's okay to feel...', 'You deserve...'), reframing/perspective-taking observations about a conflict, and enumerated actionable tips ('Practice mindfulness', 'Avoid being confrontational'), along with the numbered/bolded list markers ('2.', '4. **') that structure these advice lists. Included sentences validate emotions, normalize behavior, assign responsibility among parties in a dispute, or offer a discrete coping/communication strategy, typically in a warm, hedged, second-person advisory tone. It does not include neutral factual statements, narrative descriptions of events unconnected to advice-giving, or purely informational content (e.g., dog breed facts, government links) that lack this validating/advisory framing, even though a few such outliers appear among top activations, likely due to co-occurring list-structure formatting.

title: Transition into enumerated list of reasons or suggestions
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic lead-in phrases (often followed by a numbered list marker like '1.' or '1. **') that signal the model is about to enumerate reasons, suggestions, tips, or considerations, such as 'Here's why:', 'Here are some thoughts to consider:', 'Here's what I would suggest:', and similar preambles including transitional 'Here's where things get tricky' style hooks. The cluster includes these introductory framing sentences themselves and the bare numeral/bullet markers that immediately follow them (e.g., '1.', '2. **'), which co-activate as part of the same list-initiation pattern. It does NOT include the substantive content of the list items (the actual reasons, advice, or judgments given), nor does it include unrelated advice-giving or verdict sentences (e.g., 'you're not the asshole') that lack this explicit enumerative lead-in or numbered marker structure.

title: Recommending professional or social support-seeking
description: This latent fires on advice-genre sentences that recommend seeking help from a therapist, counselor, or trusted friend/family member to process emotions, gain perspective, or develop coping strategies. The highest-activating examples are formulaic 'they/a therapist can help you work through X and develop Y (coping strategies/a plan)' constructions, or direct imperatives like 'Consider talking to a therapist/trusted friend about your feelings.' It specifically captures the recommendation to outsource emotional processing to a third party (professional or personal support network), not general advice-giving about resolving a situation oneself. Excluded are sentences advising direct conversation with the person actually involved in the conflict (e.g., 'talk to your girlfriend/boyfriend/sibling'), which instead center on interpersonal communication/negotiation rather than seeking outside emotional support.
